title: Pattern Printing 1: Stars and Triangles
learningGoals: use a row table (row number → how many stars) to plan any pattern
print a left triangle and an inverted triangle with nested loops
right-align a triangle using a separate spaces loop
match the width of a space to the width of a star

youtube.title: The Star Pattern Exam Question, Solved | C Programming EP 31
youtube.description: Every C exam has a star pattern question. The secret is not memorising code: it is making a small row table first. We build a triangle, flip it upside down, push it to the right, and fix the spacing bug that turns a triangle into a pyramid. 0:00 Challenge answer and hook 0:30 The row table trick 1:20 Left triangle, line by line 2:45 Upside-down triangle 3:35 Right-aligned triangle 5:10 Bug of the Day: wrong spaces 6:20 Challenge

scenes.onScreen: EP 30 challenge: 3×5 grid of `#`, then an exam paper with "Print this pattern" and a star triangle
scenes.animation: Grid prints; exam paper slides in, dramatic sting
scenes.narration: Last challenge: read rows and columns, then print a grid of hashes. Outer loop for rows, inner loop for columns, and a newline after each row. Three by five gives three lines of five hashes. Hold on to that grid. Because this question, "print the following pattern", appears in almost every C exam. And once you know the trick, it is free marks.
Episode thirty-one. Pattern printing, part one.

scenes.onScreen: Row table: row 1 → 1 star, row 2 → 2 … row 5 → 5; rule "stars = i"
scenes.animation: Table rows appear beside the triangle; arrow links each row to its stars
scenes.narration: Here is the trick. Don't look at the whole pattern. Look at it row by row, and make a little table. Row 1 has 1 star. Row 2 has 2 stars. Row 3, 3 stars. Row 5, 5 stars. So the rule is: in row i, print i stars. Outer loop: which row am I on. Inner loop: how many stars in this row. Every pattern in this episode and the next is just a different row table.

scenes.animation: Stars drop in one by one; inner loop limit `j <= i` glows each row
scenes.narration: [HL 4] int n equals 5, the height. [HL 6] Outer loop: for i from 1 to n. One round per row. [TRACK i=1] [HL 7] Inner loop: for j from 1 to i. This is the rule from our table: row i has i stars. On row 1, j goes from 1 to 1, so one star. [HL 8] printf star space. [HL 10] After the inner loop, printf newline. Row 1 done: one star. [TRACK i=2] Row 2: j goes 1 to 2, two stars, then newline. [TRACK i=3] Row 3: three stars. And so on until row 5, five stars. Compare this with last episode's grid. The only change is the inner limit: j less than or equal to i, instead of j less than or equal to cols. That one change turns a rectangle into a triangle.

scenes.animation: Triangle flips upside down with a whoosh; tracker `i` 5 → 1
scenes.narration: Now flip it. Row table: row 1 has 5 stars, row 2 has 4, down to 1. [HL 6] The easy way: make the outer loop count down. for i equals n, i greater than or equal to 1, i minus minus. [TRACK i=5] [HL 7] The inner loop stays the same: j from 1 to i. So the first row prints 5 stars, [TRACK i=4] then 4, then 3, then 2, [TRACK i=1] then 1. One small change, and the triangle stands on its head.

scenes.animation: Xecxec with stars circling his head, rimshot
scenes.narration: Why did the star pattern pass the exam? Because it knew its place, row by row.

scenes.onScreen: `rt4.c` right-aligned triangle; row table now has two columns: spaces and stars
scenes.animation: Spaces drawn as dotted grey boxes, stars in Tomato; each row shows "2 spaces per missing star"
scenes.narration: Now the harder one: a triangle leaning against the right wall. The stars are the same, 1, 2, 3, 4. But each row has empty space on the left. Our row table gets a second column. With n equals 4: row 1 has 3 missing stars, row 2 has 2, row 3 has 1, row 4 has none. So missing stars equals n minus i. [HL 6] Outer loop: i from 1 to n. [TRACK i=1] [HL 7] First inner loop: for s from 1 to n minus i. This one prints the blank space. [HL 8] printf, and in quotes, two spaces. Why two? Because each star we print is a star plus a space, which is two characters wide. So each missing star must be filled with two spaces. [HL 10] Second inner loop: for j from 1 to i, [HL 11] print star space. [HL 13] Then newline. Row 1: three gaps of two spaces, then one star. [TRACK i=2] Row 2: two gaps, two stars. [TRACK i=4] Row 4: no gaps, four stars. Two inner loops, one after the other, inside one outer loop. First the spaces, then the stars.

scenes.onScreen: `printf(" ")` instead of `printf("  ")`: a pyramid appears instead
scenes.animation: Butter frame; triangle collapses into a pyramid; measuring tape shows `"* "` = 2 chars vs `" "` = 1 char
scenes.narration: Today's bug: wrong spaces. Take the right-aligned triangle, and change the two spaces in line 8 to one space. Compile: no error. Run it. Surprise! Instead of a right-aligned triangle, we get a pyramid, nicely centred. Why? Each star is two characters wide, star plus space, but each gap is now only one character wide. So the gaps are half as wide as they should be, and the stars shift to the middle. The fix: the width of a gap must match the width of a star. Star space needs two spaces. Hold on to this accident, though. Next episode, we'll build pyramids on purpose.

scenes.onScreen: "Print the upside-down right-aligned triangle" with target picture
scenes.narration: Your challenge: print this upside-down right-aligned triangle, with n equals 4. Four stars on top, then three, two, one, all touching the right wall. Hint: start from the right-aligned triangle and make the outer loop count down.
Next episode: pyramids and number patterns, crab-style. Keep coding, says Xecxec!

bug.why: Each star is printed as `"* "` (2 characters), so each missing star must be filled with 2 spaces, not 1.

shorts.title: The Exam Question Everyone Fears
shorts.script: "Print the following pattern." Every C exam has it. Here's the secret: don't look at the whole triangle. Make a row table. Row 1, one star. Row 2, two stars. Row i, i stars. Now the code writes itself. Full episode on Koding Konkani.
shorts.onScreen: EXAM QUESTION / MAKE A ROW TABLE / ROW i = i STARS
shorts.caption: Free marks in every C exam.

shorts.title: Star Triangle in 30 Seconds
shorts.script: Outer loop: for i from 1 to 5, one round per row. Inner loop: for j from 1 to i, because row i has i stars. Print star space. After the inner loop, a newline. That's the triangle. Change the inner limit from a fixed number to i, and a rectangle becomes a triangle.
shorts.onScreen: for i: ROWS / for j <= i: STARS
shorts.caption: One change: rectangle to triangle.

shorts.title: I Wanted a Triangle and Got a Pyramid
shorts.script: I wanted a triangle on the right. I got a pyramid in the middle. Why? Each star prints as star plus space, two characters wide. But I filled each gap with one space. Gaps half as wide, stars slide to the centre. Use two spaces, and the triangle snaps back to the right.
shorts.caption: The happiest accident in C.

shorts.title: Pun: Knows Its Place
shorts.hook: Xecxec dizzy with stars around his head

shorts.title: What Does This Print?
shorts.script: Same triangle code, but instead of a star, we print j. What do you get? Row 1: 1. Row 2: 1 2. Row 3: 1 2 3. Up to 1 2 3 4 5. A number triangle, for free. Comment if you guessed it.
shorts.caption: Stars to numbers in one change.
